title: Kneeling Emoji 🧎 Meaning: Begging, Worship and “On My Knees”
description: The kneeling emoji 🧎 shows a person on their knees. Online it means begging, being floored by someone’s talent or looks, prayer, or a sexual hint.
summary: 🧎 depicts a person kneeling upright. People use it to beg or plead, to show they are overwhelmed with admiration (“on my knees for this”), and for literal kneeling in prayer, proposals or protest. It can also carry a sexual implication. The meaning depends heavily on what it follows.
meaning: The kneeling person arrived in 2019 as a plain depiction of a posture, alongside a standing person. Its literal uses are varied: praying, proposing marriage, gardening, yoga, waiting, or taking a knee in protest. For those, the emoji is descriptive and neutral, and religious users in particular rely on it for prayer and worship posts. Nothing in the design points to any one of these, so the surrounding words decide.

Internet slang gave it a louder life. In fan and stan communities, being “on my knees” means being so impressed, attracted or emotionally wrecked that you cannot stand. 🧎 expresses that collapse: “the bridge of this song 🧎,” “her in that suit 🧎‍♀️.” It works as submission to greatness, similar to bowing down, and is usually exaggerated for comic effect.

Begging is the other everyday sense. “Please drop the tour dates 🧎” or “one more episode, I’m begging 🧎” put the sender on their knees in front of an artist, a company or a friend. It adds desperation and humor to requests, especially when repeated in a row as if a crowd were pleading. The plea is rarely expected to work; it is a way of showing how much the sender cares.

Because of what kneeling can imply, the emoji is also used suggestively, to allude to oral sex or to sexual submission, often pointed toward another emoji or a name. That reading is common in thirst comments. The line between “I admire you” and something cruder is thin here, so audience matters more than with most people emojis. When unsure how it will be taken, 🙏 or 🙇 expresses admiration or pleading with less risk.

contexts.label: On TikTok and Instagram
contexts.body: This is its home turf. Comments under concert clips, celebrity photos and fan edits are full of 🧎 as a sign of devotion or thirst. It also features in pleading comments asking creators for a part two or brands for a restock. The facing-right versions let people aim the kneeling figure at whatever comes next.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Friends use it to beg dramatically (“please come with me 🧎”) or to react to something so good it knocked them down. Between partners it may be flirtatious or explicit. If someone sends it with 🙏 or a religious message, they simply mean they are praying. As always with this emoji, the relationship tells you which reading is intended.

contexts.label: In faith and ceremony
contexts.body: Christians, Muslims and others use 🧎 for prayer, worship and humility before God, often with 🙏 or a place of worship. It appears in proposal announcements as the partner on one knee, although the figure is on both knees in most designs. In sports and activism it can reference kneeling as protest.

examples.meaning: Dramatically begging an artist for new music.

examples.text: That high note at the end 🧎‍♀️
examples.meaning: So impressed by a performance that she has figuratively collapsed.
Literal reference to kneeling in prayer.

examples.text: He asked and I said yes!! 🧎‍♂️💍
Can you pleeease cover my shift 🧎
examples.meaning: Pleading with a friend or coworker for a favor.
Expressing strong attraction, with a suggestive undertone.

combos.meaning: Desperate pleading or being emotionally destroyed by something good.
Worshipping someone or something, usually as fan hyperbole.

confusedWith.difference: 🙇 is a deep bow with the head lowered, rooted in Japanese apology and gratitude. 🧎 stays upright on the knees and is used for begging, awe, prayer and innuendo.
🙏 shows only pressed palms for please, thanks or prayer and is safe almost anywhere. 🧎 involves the whole body and can read as suggestive, so it is riskier in mixed company.
🧍 is a figure standing stiffly, popular for awkwardness and “just standing there.” The two were released together, but 🧎 conveys submission or pleading rather than discomfort.

avoid: Do not send it to coworkers or acquaintances as a reaction to their appearance, because the sexual reading is widely known.
Avoid using it jokingly in religious discussions where kneeling is a sincere act of worship.
Leave it out of messages to anyone who might take “on my knees” literally and feel uncomfortable.
design: The emoji shows a full-body figure in profile, resting on both knees with the torso upright and arms at the sides. By default it faces left on most platforms, and right-facing versions were added in Emoji 15.1. Clothing color varies by vendor. Woman 🧎‍♀️ and man 🧎‍♂️ variants and five skin tones are available.

faqs.a: It usually means “I’m on my knees,” an exaggerated way to say you are begging for something or overwhelmed by how good or attractive someone is. In flirtatious or explicit contexts it can also imply sexual submission or oral sex.

faqs.q: What does 🧎‍♀️ mean from a girl?
faqs.a: Most often she is being dramatic about how much she loves something or wants something: a song, a celebrity, a favor. If it is aimed at you after a photo, she is saying you look extremely good, possibly with suggestive intent.

faqs.q: What does 🧎‍♂️ mean from a guy?
faqs.a: He may be pleading, joking about worshipping something impressive, praying, or referencing a proposal. Sent in response to your picture, it means he is floored by how you look, and it can be a forward, sexual compliment depending on the tone of the chat.

faqs.q: Is the kneeling emoji used for prayer?
faqs.a: Yes. Many people use it sincerely for prayer and worship, often with 🙏. There is also 🛐, the place of worship symbol, which shows a kneeling figure under a roof and is strictly religious in meaning.

It was introduced in Emoji 12.0 in 2019 together with a standing person and several accessibility-related emojis, such as people using wheelchairs and canes. Versions facing right were added later in Emoji 15.1.
